one_liner: Pure safe-Rust rewrite of libxml2 (parse, DOM, SAX, XPath, DTD, C14N) whose CLI parses faster than xmllint as shipped.
what_it_does: A new implementation of libxml2 in Rust, not a binding. It covers XML 1.0 parsing into an arena DOM, SAX2, a pull reader, save/writer, XPath 1.0, DTD validation, C14N, XInclude, HTML, and partial RelaxNG/XSD/Schematron. The API mirrors libxml2 in snake_case (xmlReadMemory becomes xml_read_memory, with #[doc(alias)] entries and the same numeric XML_PARSE_* bits), so C code ports over by hand but nothing links against it: the C-ABI cdylib is still a stub. The rxmlint CLI takes the same flags as xmllint.
how_it_is_fast: About half of the published margin comes from the allocator. rxmlint uses rusty_alloc, a pure-Rust port of mimalloc, as its #[global_allocator], while xmllint runs on the system allocator. The rest comes from ordinary scanner work in the 0.2.0 performance release: character data and attribute values are copied in one pass per ASCII run instead of decoding each character, names are scanned in place as byte spans, UTF-8 decoding checks only the leading scalar (this fixed an O(n^2) re-validation), scratch attribute vectors are reused, and the arena DOM uses u32 NodeId handles. Allocations on the attribute-heavy file fell 72%. There is no SIMD and no string interning: every node and attribute still holds owned Strings, which explains why the allocator matters so much.
when_to_use: You need libxml2's feature set (XPath 1.0, DTD validation, C14N/exclusive C14N, HTML parsing) in a Rust or wasm32 build with no C toolchain, no *-sys crate and #![forbid(unsafe_code)] throughout.
You parse untrusted XML and want no-network and no-XXE behaviour that cannot be switched off, plus bounded entity expansion.
Your binary already uses rusty_alloc (or you are willing to set it as the global allocator). The as-shipped 1.55x-2.31x DOM-parse gain over xmllint depends on it.
You parse attribute-heavy documents of hundreds of KB to MB into a DOM. big-attr.xml is the only large file that stays faster (about 1.25x) when both sides use the same allocator.
You are porting libxml2-based code to Rust and want the same function names and option bits.
when_not_to_use: You need a parser that is faster on its own merits. With the same allocator the author measures 0.80x on big-attr and 1.07x (slower) on big-300k, and the board has not been re-run since rxmlint 0.2.0. The 0.3.0 through 0.8.1 conformance releases have landed since then.

You need streaming or bounded memory. xml_reader_for_memory and rxmlint --stream build the whole tree and then walk it. Only the rusty_xml-specific XML_PARSE_NO_TREE flag with a SAX handler avoids building nodes.
You need XML 1.1, external entity or DTD loading, gzip input (XML_PARSE_UNZIP is not wired), or Shift_JIS/EUC-JP/ISO-2022-JP encodings. None of these are supported.
You need a C-ABI drop-in for libxml2 (the cdylib is a stub) or the full RelaxNG/XSD/Schematron validators (only working subsets exist).

You need a mature dependency. The repo was created 2026-08-27, versions 0.1.0 to 0.8.1 all shipped within three days, it has 1 star and about 268 crates.io downloads, and every commit since 0.8.1 has been a README edit.

integration.dependencies: none outside its own workspace crates for the library. rxmlint alone pulls in rusty_alloc-api (plus libc/windows-sys) through rusty_xml-alloc. cargo-deny bans *-sys crates and copyleft.
integration.platforms: Windows x86-64, Linux and macOS are built and tested in CI. The wasm32-unknown-unknown library passes cargo check in CI. No arch-specific code or SIMD.
integration.thread_safety: not documented. XmlDoc is plain owned data (Vec/String/HashMap, no Rc/RefCell/unsafe) and xml_init_parser is a no-op with no global state, so separate documents on separate threads should be fine.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the Rust API mirrors libxml2 names and XML_PARSE_* bits and rxmlint takes xmllint's flags, but there is no C ABI, the output diverges on entity-reference nodes and DTD-subset serialization, and NONET|NO_XXE are always forced on

gotchas: The library never sets #[global_allocator]. Linked into your app on the system allocator, you get the same-allocator result (0.80x-1.07x of libxml2), not the headline 0.43x-0.64x.
xml_ctxt_use_options ORs in XML_PARSE_NONET | XML_PARSE_NO_XXE on every call, so documents that depend on external entities or DTDs cannot be loaded, even when you pass other flags.

Without NOENT, general entities are expanded where libxml2 keeps entity-reference nodes, and the internal DTD subset is serialized verbatim where C reorders it. Tree shape and byte output differ from xmllint in these two cases.
Since 0.2.0 the pub `name` field of #text/#comment/#cdata-section/#document nodes is an empty String. Use XmlDoc::name() to get the canonical name.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rusty_xml when you need libxml2's breadth (XPath, DTD validation, C14N, HTML) in memory-safe pure Rust. If raw parse speed is the goal, the C/C++ siblings beat libxml2 by much more: RapidXml at 1084.9 vs 278.8 MB/s DOM, SpeedyXml at 4.4x streaming, and libleptris at 1.4-3.6x.
verified_claims_summary: This is an author-run, CLI-vs-CLI comparison on Windows: rxmlint 0.2.0 (release build, rustc not stated, linked with rusty_alloc) against a pinned MSVC build of libxml2 v2.15.3 xmllint on the system allocator. Both parsed with --noout --repeat, pinned to one core, measuring CPU time over 20 ABBA pairs; the CPU model is not stated. rusty_xml was 1.55x-2.31x faster on four files (83.25 vs 37.18 MB/s on big-attr), but with the same allocator on both sides it was only about 1.25x faster on big-attr and about 7% slower on big-300k. The slashdot row is inflated because xmllint re-reads the file on every repeat.
status_note: The last code release was 0.8.1 on 2026-08-29, and every commit since has been a README edit (the 'active installs' count is self-reported). It is MIT OR Apache-2.0, 100% safe Rust and on crates.io, but the whole project was written in under a month by a single maintainer org.
